Senses.Explanation: Budai, literally "the Cloth-Bag monk," is the non-lineage figure defined in Chan records by the bag he carries and uses in public exchanges. His title occurs 200 times in 105 allowlisted texts. Asked "what is the cloth bag?" (如何是布袋), he puts the bag down; asked "what is the matter beneath the cloth bag?" (如何是布袋下事), he shoulders it and leaves. Asked the great meaning of the buddha-teaching, he again puts it down and stands with folded hands; asked whether there is an upward matter, he shoulders it and goes. In the street he says he is waiting for a person and rejects the monk who claims to have arrived. Later records quote his verse, "Maitreya, true Maitreya, divides into hundreds of thousands of bodies, constantly showing himself to people, while people do not recognize him" (彌勒真彌勒，分身千百億，時時示時人，時人自不識), then comment on it. The Zen Budai is thus the bag-bearing street monk whose putting down, shouldering, waiting, and Maitreya verse are repeatedly raised and judged.
Senses.Note: One person/title sense. The bag itself (布袋) is a related concrete headword, not a second sense of the full title. The corpus identifies the figure through the bag and the Maitreya verse; this entry adds no outside life story.

Senses.Explanation: (會) to understand / get + (麼) (final interrogative particle): "do you get it?" A stock closing challenge (6053 occ / 367 texts). The dominant frame is "do you still get it?" (還會麼; 2085 occ / 270 texts); it is addressed to the assembly as (大眾會麼) (261) and (諸人會麼) (48). The recurring pattern: a master presents something — a saying, a raised case, a held-up object, or an abrupt action — and then asks (還會麼); the question is frequently followed by (良久) (a pause) and a further line, e.g. (還會麼良久云三邊若得渾無事) and (召大眾云還會麼良久擲如意云); or the interlocutor answers "I don't get it" (不會), e.g. (陛下還會麼)。(帝曰)。(不會) and (拈起帽子兩帶曰)。(還會麼)。(曰)。(不會). In a public encounter a teacher overturns the dining table, asks (會麼), and judges the lecturer's answer "table"; Yunmen sharpens the same question to (驢年會麼), "will you get it in the year of the donkey?" It also stands as the pivot before a verdict — "do you get it? if not yet…" (諸人還會麼。其或未然) — and closes an address, (良久曰)：(還會麼)？(珍重). The texts use it as a discourse marker and assign it no further gloss, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide discourse marker. Most curated occurrences are the stock question posed by an unnamed (師) or into the assembly; Yunmen's marked (驢年會麼) is safely attributed but remains the same understand-question, not a master-specific sense. The reciprocal reply in the record is (不會). Counts: (會麼) 6053/367; (還會麼) 2085/270; (大眾會麼) 261; (諸人會麼) 48.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to differ by a little; in the records, to be somewhat closer or a little better by comparison. The phrase occurs 854 times in 224 allowlisted texts. It is a recurrent, often qualified appraisal: Huangbo says that among Mazu's eighty-four teachers only Guizong is somewhat closer; Wuye says a monk who tries to help is somewhat closer; another master replies that the student's not understanding is a little closer. Yuanwu says that being entirely unlike a list of proposed identifications is only then somewhat closer, and immediately asks why. The phrase can also qualify silence, withdrawal, or the condition before a question, while still withholding full approval.
Senses.Note: The Chan deployment turns an ordinary small comparison into a clipped public verdict: 'closer' regularly does not mean accepted or complete. The texts supply the compared speech or action and retain the phrase as a comparative appraisal. All occurrences are comparative appraisals of the same kind, so no sense split is warranted.
